_about: Swiss wine regions and communal appellations below the cantonal AOC, read by pipeline/ch_regions.py. Outlines are the union of the listed communes (BFS GEOSTAT generalised boundaries, swiss-maps 4.7.0; 'year' picks an older boundary set for former communes). 'point' places are drawn as a marker. Every figure carries its source in 'refs'. Editorial text is CC BY 4.0, Open Wine Atlas contributors.

ch-canton-18.area_note: 422.2 ha in the Rhine valley and Brusio plus 27.9 ha in the Misox, 2025 (BLW, Das Weinjahr 2025)
ch-canton-18.basis: Kantonale Weinverordnung BR 917.400 (in force since 1 March 2018)
ch-canton-18.grape_share_note: Share of the 422 ha in the Rhine valley and Brusio, Plantahof Rebbaustatistik 2025 (55 varieties in all). The Misox grows mostly Merlot.
ch-canton-18.atlas_note: Switzerland's Pinot Noir stronghold: two thirds of the vines are Blauburgunder. The warm Föhn wind from the south, called the grape cooker, gives long ripe autumns in a valley sheltered by the Rätikon. Four villages of the Bündner Herrschaft hold about 83% of the vineyards. The law names three wine areas: the Bündner Rheintal, the Misox south of the Alps and Brusio in the Valposchiavo.

ch-canton-22.grape_share_note: Chasselas about 60% of the area in 2018, down from 71% in 1994 (Statistique Vaud, Numerus 2019)
ch-canton-22.basis: Règlement sur les vins vaudois (RVV), RSV 916.125.2
ch-canton-22.atlas_note: The second wine canton of Switzerland and the home of Chasselas. Six regional AOCs, Chablais, Lavaux, La Côte, Côtes de l'Orbe, Bonvillars and Vully, and two grand cru appellations, Dézaley and Calamin, inside Lavaux. The terraces of Lavaux are a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2007. Since 2010 the best parcels can earn the cantonal mention Premier grand cru.
ch-canton-22.pgc_rule: Premier grand cru (since 2010): a named clos, château, domaine or lieu-dit approved by the cantonal commission, hand harvest, at least 6,000 vines/ha, Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamay, Merlot, Gamaret or Garanoir, no blending, bottled in Vaud

ch-canton-25.area_note: 1,246.3 ha in Switzerland and 117.4 ha in the French border zone (Viry, Challex, Saint-Julien and others), 2024. 56% red.
ch-canton-25.basis: Règlement sur la vigne et les vins, RSG M 2 50.05
ch-canton-25.label_rule: Commune name on the label: at least 85% of the grapes from that commune (RSG M 2 50.05 art. 58)
ch-canton-25.atlas_note: The first AOC of Switzerland, created in 1988, and the third wine canton. Three areas: the Rive droite or Mandement with Satigny, the largest wine commune of the country, Entre Arve et Rhône and Entre Arve et Lac. Gamay, not Chasselas, is the first grape. Half the vineyard is in 23 premiers crus, defined parcels of at least about 1 ha with lower yields.
ch-canton-25.premiers_crus_note: 23 premiers crus with 685.8 ha, OCAN Genève 2024. Yields at most 1.0 kg/m² for Chasselas and Riesling-Sylvaner, 0.9 kg/m² for the others.
refs: Règlement sur la vigne et les vins, RSG M 2 50.05

ch-canton-23.area_note: 45,777,472 m2 in 2025: 1,931.6 ha white (42%) and 2,646.1 ha red (58%), down 38 ha on 2024 (BLW). The cantonal wine office gives 4,564 ha and 62 wine communes on its own page. About 18,225 people own vineyard in the register.
ch-canton-23.grape_share_note: Hectares for Valais in BLW, Das Weinjahr 2025, tables 1.2 and 1.3 (given there in ares). The canton page gives Pinot Noir 26.6%, Chasselas 16.0% and Gamay 9.4%, together 52% of the vineyard. Amigne, Humagne Blanche, Humagne Rouge and Cornalin are grown almost only in Valais.
ch-canton-23.basis: Ordonnance sur la vigne et le vin (OVV), RS VS 916.142, of 17 March 2004 (consolidated version in force 1 April 2026)
ch-canton-23.label_rule: Commune name on the label: at least 85% of the grapes from the commune and the rest from neighbouring communes; 'Ville de' or 'Village de' may precede it (OVV art. 63). Neighbouring communes with a uniform natural setting may share a regional name with the service's approval, but names like 'district de Sion' are banned (art. 64). A local name from the official survey may be used (art. 68).
ch-canton-23.atlas_note: The largest wine canton of Switzerland, about a third of the national vineyard, along the dry upper Rhône valley from Lake Geneva to Brig. Pinot Noir, Chasselas sold as Fendant and Gamay cover half the vines; Sylvaner, Petite Arvine, Heida, Syrah, Cornalin and Humagne Rouge follow. There is one cantonal AOC. Below it a wine can name its commune, and a dozen communes have their own Grand Cru rules. The law knows no premier cru: the word is banned on Valais labels.

rules: Grand Cru (OVV art. 85 to 97): set by a communal or regional regulation homologated by the Conseil d'Etat, one per commune or region. Only Chasselas, Sylvaner, Amigne, Arvine, Marsanne, Roussanne, Savagnin, Humagne Blanc, Pinot Gris, Rèze, Pinot Noir, Gamay, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge and Syrah. Yield at most 1.1 kg/m2 for Chasselas, 1.0 for Sylvaner, 0.8 for the rest; vines at least eight years old; no blending of varieties or vintages; vinified and bottled in Valais. The label shows Grand Cru, the commune or region and the vintage; 'Grand Cru Valais', 'premier cru' and 'cru classé' are banned. Cornalin, Humagne Rouge and Syrah not before 1 April of the second year. The IVV control rules add the common Valais bottle and a tasting minimum of 84/100.

Fendant = Chasselas, Johannisberg = Sylvaner, Malvoisie = Pinot Gris, Ermitage = Marsanne and/or Roussanne, Païen or Heida = Savagnin Blanc, Dôle = Pinot Noir alone or at least 85% Pinot Noir with Gamay, Dôle Blanche and Oeil de Perdrix are rosés, Goron is a red vin de pays without place name (OVV art. 49 to 61)

ch-canton-21.area_note: 88% red, 12% white, 2025, canton Ticino only. With the Mesolcina the cantonal office counts 1,143 ha for Italian-speaking Switzerland in 2025, of which 855 ha (74.8%) Merlot.
ch-canton-21.basis: Regolamento sulla viticoltura (RViti), RL 916.150 of 11 Sept 2024, art. 16 to 18, and the Direttive sulla viticoltura of 13 Sept 2024 (point 3, DOC; point 5, IGT), on the federal Weinverordnung SR 916.140. The 2015 regulation, which held the DOC rules, was repealed in 2024.
ch-canton-21.label_rule: 'Ticino' plus a grape variety: at least 90% of that variety. Blends: 'Rosso, Bianco or Rosato del Ticino', naming the main variety and others above 10%, never a single variety. 'Denominazione di origine controllata' in full on the main label, right after the name. Part of canton, district, commune, frazione or land register name may be added if on the production and harvest control certificates; not on non-vintage DOC in 1, 0.5 or 0.2 l bottles with crown or screw cap. 'Castello' only for land with that name in the land register for 20 years. Riserva needs the vintage (Direttive 2024, 3.1, 3.10, 3.13, 3.14).
ch-canton-21.grapes: Red: Bondola / Cabernet Franc / Cabernet Sauvignon / Carminoir / Diolinoir / Divico / Galotta / Gamaret / Garanoir / Marselan / Merlot / Petit Verdot / Pinot Nero / Syrah. White: Chardonnay / Chasselas / Doral / Johanniter / Kerner / Müller-Thurgau / Pinot Bianco / Pinot Grigio / Sauvignon Bianco / Sauvignon Grigio / Semillon / Viognier. Up to 10% of other registered varieties, not named on the label.
ch-canton-21.atlas_note: The wine canton of Italian-speaking Switzerland, and Merlot country: about three quarters of the vines are Merlot. It came after phylloxera, when the first cuttings were handed out in 1906 and Bondola, the old local red, was replaced. The Monte Ceneri pass splits the canton into the Sopraceneri and the Sottoceneri, and the Mendrisio district alone has over a third of the vines. Nearly a third of the Merlot is now pressed as white wine.
ch-canton-21.producers_note: Gambero Rosso Tre Bicchieri 2021: Paolo Basso Wine (Lugano), Angelo Delea (Losone). The Cantina Sociale Mendrisio, founded 1949, has about 350 member growers (ticino.ch).

rules: Nostrano is a traditional name of the IGT tier, not DOC. Any variety registered in the vineyard cadastre of Ticino or the Mesolcina may be used, including the American and hybrid grapes that are banned from DOC blending and from other IGT wine (RViti 2024 art. 18; Direttive 2024 point 5 and annex 1). Swiss Wine notes Bondola is often blended into Nostrano.

Americana is the local name for American grapes and direct-producer hybrids such as Isabella, Clinton and Noah. Annex 1 of the 2024 directives excludes them from DOC and from IGT, except as Nostrano. The 2024 statistics count 42.9 ha of red American and hybrid varieties plus 4.8 ha of Isabella in the canton, most of it in the Locarnese, the Luganese and the Valle Maggia.

Much Merlot is pressed as a white wine. In 2023, 1,491,354 kg of Merlot, 29% of the Merlot harvest, was vinified white; in 2024, 43.4 ha were registered as Merlot for Blanc de Noir. The law has no separate category for it: it is DOC Ticino like any other white, and growers must declare red grapes vinified white (RViti 2024 art. 11).

DOC grapes may come from Ticino and the Mesolcina (GR) and must be vinified in Ticino or the Mesolcina. Minimum natural sugar 18.0 Brix for red and 16.0 Brix for white; maximum yield 1,000 g/m2 red and 1,200 g/m2 white. Up to 10% blending, never with red or rosé wine from outside the canton (Direttive 2024, 3.3 to 3.8).
Growers in Ticino 2023, including 111 from outside the canton with vines in Ticino; plus 93 in the Mesolcina. 185 wineries vinified grapes in 2023 (Rapporto vendemmia 2023).
2025: 37,903 hl of wine in Ticino, 14,003 hl white and 23,900 hl red; 10,240 hl of the white was made from red grapes (BLW, Das Weinjahr 2025).

ch-canton-24.area_note: 382.8 ha red (63%) and 220.5 ha white (37%), 2025. The legal vineyard zone (zone viticole) was enlarged to 556 ha in March 2018 (Plan directeur cantonal, fiche S_23).
ch-canton-24.grape_share_note: Hectares 2025 from BLW, Das Weinjahr 2025, tables 1.2 and 1.3 (read from the NE column). Neuchâtel Vins et Terroir gives similar figures: Pinot Noir 334 ha, Chasselas 150 ha, Chardonnay 26 ha, Pinot Gris 24 ha, Gamaret 14 ha, Garanoir 9 ha.
ch-canton-24.basis: Arrêté concernant l'appellation d'origine contrôlée des vins de Neuchâtel, RSN 916.120.1, of 20 June 2016 (annex 3 last changed 18 Aug 2021); Loi sur la viticulture RSN 916.120 (vineyard zone and cadastre)
ch-canton-24.grapes: Chardonnay / Chasselas / Doral / Gewürztraminer / Müller-Thurgau / Pinot Blanc / Pinot Gris / Sauvignon Blanc / Viognier / Gamaret / Garanoir / Pinot Noir
ch-canton-24.label_rule: One AOC, Neuchâtel. A commune, locality, region or sector name may be added if at least 85% of the grapes come from it (art. 4); a cadastral name needs 95% from parcels of that name (art. 5). The grape must be named, except for Chasselas, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine (art. 6). A Pinot Noir must hold at least 95% Pinot Noir (art. 12). Wines must be made in the canton (art. 15).
ch-canton-24.atlas_note: About 600 ha on the north shore of Lake Neuchâtel, at the foot of the Jura, from Le Landeron to Vaumarcus. Limestone soils of Jurassic origin. Pinot Noir covers more than half the vineyard, Chasselas about a quarter. Only twelve grape varieties are allowed for the AOC. The canton gave the country the Œil-de-Perdrix rosé and the unfiltered Chasselas sold each January.
ch-canton-24.producers_note: 53 winegrowers and cellars (Neuchâtel Vins et Terroir). Caves de la Ville de Neuchâtel own 13.4 ha (Hachette Vins).

rules: Grand cru is governed by a regulation of the Interprofession viti-vinicole neuchâteloise (IVN). Only still AOC Neuchâtel wines made solely from Chardonnay, Chasselas or Pinot Noir vinified red may use it. Any other quality term such as 1er Cru or Grand cru classé is banned (RSN 916.120.1 art. 14).

Minimum sugar 15.2 °Brix for Chasselas and Müller-Thurgau, 18.4 °Brix for most other still wines (annex 2). Maximum yield 0.9 kg/m² for Chasselas and Müller-Thurgau, 0.8 kg/m² for most others, 1.0 kg/m² for sparkling base (annex 3, 2021).

Chasselas AOC Neuchâtel bottled without any filtration, sold from the third Wednesday of January after the harvest (RSN 916.120.1 annex 7). First made in 1975 by Henri-Alexandre Godet. About thirty cellars make it, about 15% of the canton's Chasselas (Neuchâtel Vins et Terroir 2024).

Federal term: rosé AOC wine from Pinot Noir, with at most 10% Pinot Gris or Pinot Blanc (Ordonnance sur le vin RS 916.140, annex 1). Not reserved to Neuchâtel. First official trace in Neuchâtel 1861, a label printed by Louis Bovet, cellar owner at Areuse.

Blanc de noirs from Pinot Noir. Protected as the guarantee mark Perdrix blanche®; the 2010 AOC decree barred blending and tied its making to the mark's rules (art. 10 and 11). Not named in the 2016 decree.

ch-canton-1.area_note: 57% red, 43% white, 2025. Strickhof gave 604.6 ha of bearing vineyard for 2024.
ch-canton-1.grape_note: Read from BLW, Das Weinjahr 2025, tables 1.2 and 1.3 (Zürich column). Strickhof 2024: Blauburgunder 254 ha, Riesling-Silvaner 107.7 ha.
ch-canton-1.basis: Verordnung über den Rebbau, LS 916.51, §§ 12b to 12d: the Baudirektion sets the designations of origin and their areas; details in the Verfügung des ALN über den Rebbau
ch-canton-1.label_rule: A geographic Zusatzbezeichnung (Lage, Flurname, region, hamlet) must be on the cantonal list (Anhang 1 of the ALN Verfügung) and 100% of the wine must come from it, apart from the federal blending tolerance (Strickhof). For AOC Zürichsee a commune name needs at least 85% from that commune (Schwyz decree 2025, Ziff. 2.3, which must match the Zürich rules).
ch-canton-1.atlas_note: The largest wine canton of German-speaking Switzerland, with about 600 ha. Swiss Wine counts five regions: the Weinland in the Andelfingen district, the Unterland, the Zürichsee, Winterthur and the Limmattal. Blauburgunder covers about 42% and Riesling-Silvaner about 17%. Räuschling, called the Zürichsee vine, is the local white grape, on about 20 ha.
ch-canton-1.history_note: Benedictines brought vines to the island of Rheinau in the 9th century. In the late 19th century over 20,000 growers worked 5,600 ha (Swiss Wine).

ch-canton-14.area_note: 68% red, 2025 (BLW). The cantonal Fachstelle counts 463.48 ha planted plus 30.58 ha unplanted vineyard in 2025: 436.15 ha AOC, 25.99 ha Landwein.
ch-canton-14.grape_note: Planted area 2025, Fachstelle Rebbau SH-TG (Bericht Weinbau 2025). 34 red and 24 white varieties.
ch-canton-14.basis: Kantonale Weinverordnung, SHR 817.402 (in force 1 Dec 2009), § 10 and § 11
ch-canton-14.label_rule: Commune name: 60% of the wine from that commune and 100% from the same production area (§ 11 Abs. 2). Several communes of one area may be named together if 100% comes from them. Lage name: 100% from the site, which must be in the cantonal Reblagenverzeichnis (§ 11 Abs. 4).
ch-canton-14.atlas_note: The Blauburgunderland: Pinot Noir covers over half the vines. The law splits the canton into two production areas, the Klettgau in the west with about four fifths of the vines, and Reiat/Rhein around the city, Stein am Rhein and Buchberg. Hallau is the largest wine commune of German-speaking Switzerland. The All Saints monastery in Schaffhausen owned vines in Hallau by 1100.
refs: Fachstelle Rebbau SH-TG, Bericht über den Weinbau SH und TG, Weinbau 2025 (Feb 2026)

ch-canton-20.area_note: 59% red, 2025 (BLW). The Fachstelle counts 242.24 ha planted plus 27.39 ha unplanted in 2025: 212.13 ha AOC, 26.42 ha Landwein.
ch-canton-20.grape_note: Planted area 2025, Fachstelle Rebbau SH-TG (Bericht Weinbau 2025). 32 red and 31 white varieties.
ch-canton-20.basis: Landwirtschaftsverordnung, RB 910.11, §§ 36 to 37 and Anhänge 1 to 3
ch-canton-20.label_rule: Commune, former commune or Ortsteil from Anhang 2: 60% from that place, the rest from Thurgau (§ 36d Abs. 2). Reblage from Anhang 3: the wine must come from that site (§ 36d Abs. 3). Outside the listed names the political commune applies.
ch-canton-20.atlas_note: A small wine canton in the land of apples, with about 240 ha left from more than 2,000 ha two centuries ago. Hermann Müller, born in Thurgau, bred the Müller-Thurgau grape in 1882 and it carries the canton's name. The law groups the vines in three production areas: Unteres Thurtal, Oberes Thurtal and Untersee. Swiss Wine counts six smaller regions.
refs: Fachstelle Rebbau SH-TG, Bericht über den Weinbau SH und TG, Weinbau 2025 (Feb 2026)

ch-canton-19.area_note: 64% red, 2025 (BLW). Liebegg counted 381.3 ha and 583 growers in 2024.
ch-canton-19.grape_note: BLW, Das Weinjahr 2025, tables 1.2 and 1.3 (Aargau column)
ch-canton-19.basis: Verordnung über den Weinbau (Weinbauverordnung), SAR 915.712, § 14; Grand Cru chapter §§ 19b to 19i since 1 Jan 2025
ch-canton-19.label_rule: The whole canton is one production area (§ 14 Abs. 1). Ortschaft or commune name: at least 60% from there; region name: at least 90%; Lage name: at least 90% (§ 14 Abs. 2 to 4). Other blends are AOC Aargau. The Liebegg publishes the approved Lage names: 77 sites in 37 communes (Feb 2025).
ch-canton-19.atlas_note: About 380 ha spread over many small villages, mostly on south facing slopes of the main and side valleys. Almost 600 growers, most of them part time on under one hectare. Blauburgunder is about half the area. In the 1880s the canton had 2,700 ha of vines. Since 2025 the law has a Grand Cru Aargau for Pinot Noir.
refs: Aargau, Änderung der Weinbauverordnung vom 27.11.2024 (Grand Cru Aargau)

rules: Grand Cru Aargau (since 2025): Blauburgunder only, from approved parcels scoring 140 of 180 points, vines at least 15 years old, at most 0.6 kg/m², at least 95 °Oechsle, 12 months in barrique, no chaptalisation, 18 of 20 points at tasting, release from 1 June of the second year (SAR 915.712 §§ 19b to 19i)

ch-canton-17.area_note: 74.9 ha white, 128.9 ha red, 2025 (BLW). The cantonal harvest control lists 200.2 ha by variety in 2025.
ch-canton-17.grape_share_note: Share of the 200.2 ha in the LZSG harvest control 2025: Blauburgunder 96.1 ha, Müller-Thurgau 17.9 ha, Chardonnay 12.2 ha, Sauvignon Blanc 9.6 ha, Johanniter 9.2 ha, Merlot 5.6 ha, Pinot Gris 3.6 ha, Zweigelt 3.4 ha. Over 70 varieties in all.
ch-canton-17.label_rule: AOC St.Gallen: at least 90% of the grapes from the canton (Art. 35). Production area name: 100% from it; commune name: at least 60% from the commune, the rest from the same production area; named part of a commune: it must hold two thirds of the commune's vines and give 60% of the grapes; single site: 100% (Art. 41a).
ch-canton-17.subregions: Four production areas (Art. 41a Abs. 2): St.Galler Rheintal, Sarganserland (or Sarganserland-Walensee / Walensee for the lakeside communes), Zürichsee (only together with the commune name) and Fürstenland.
ch-canton-17.atlas_note: Most of the vines are in the St. Gallen Rhine valley and the Sarganserland, on steep south slopes. Blauburgunder covers about half the area. Berneck is the largest wine commune, and Pfäfers has the highest vineyard of eastern Switzerland at 740 m. Wine from Appenzell is checked by the same cantonal office in the harvest control.

ch-canton-13.grape_share_note: Ebenrain harvest control 2025, share of the 114.0 ha (BLW): Blauburgunder 52.9 ha, Riesling-Silvaner 10.7 ha, Kerner 5.1 ha, Sauvignon Blanc 4.8 ha, Chardonnay 3.1 ha, Pinot Gris 2.9 ha. BL, BS and SO together grow 83 varieties; 18.6% of the area is fungus resistant (interspecific) varieties.
ch-canton-13.basis: Verordnung über den Pflanzenbau SGS 516.31, §§ 10-22 (Stand 1 May 2025); the Ebenrain centre in Sissach runs the vineyard register for BL, BS and SO
ch-canton-13.label_rule: AOC Basel-Landschaft; Baselbieter Wein if the grapes come from the BL production area. Commune or registered regional name: at least 70% of the grapes from it, at most 30% from other communes of the same production area. Site (Lage): 100%, and the site must be in the cantonal Reblagenverzeichnis (§ 12).
ch-canton-13.atlas_note: Vines on the south slopes of the Tafeljura and Faltenjura east and south of Basel. Blauburgunder is almost half the area, Riesling-Silvaner and Kerner lead the whites. Aesch, Maisprach, Sissach and Muttenz are the largest wine communes.

ch-canton-3.area_note: 53.4 ha white, 37.9 ha red, 2025 (BLW). About 10 ha in the 1980s (SRF 2025).
ch-canton-3.piwi_note: Fungus resistant (PIWI) varieties: over 45% of the area in 2025, against 3.5% in Switzerland (canton of Luzern via zentralplus, Nov 2025)
ch-canton-3.basis: Verordnung über die kontrollierte Ursprungsbezeichnung für Weine SRL 917 (7 July 2009)
ch-canton-3.label_rule: KUB Luzern or AOC Luzern on the main label. Region, commune or site may be added; a blend of regions may name only the canton, a blend of communes only canton and region (§ 3). Varieties making up at least 85% of the wine are listed in order (§ 4).
ch-canton-3.subregions: Four wine regions (§ 2): Seetal, Surental/Sempachersee, Vierwaldstättersee and Wiggertal. The ordinance does not list their communes.
ch-canton-3.atlas_note: A young wine canton that grew from about 10 ha in the 1980s to over 90 ha. Vines grow around the lakes of Lucerne, Sempach, Hallwil and Baldegg and in the lower Wiggertal. Close to half the area is fungus resistant varieties such as Solaris and Divico, far above the Swiss average of 3.5%. The AOC dates from 2005.

d.atlas_note: Four villages under the Falknis and the Rätikon, the best known Pinot Noir address of Switzerland. Pinot Noir came from Burgundy around 1630, probably with Bündner mercenaries, and Schloss Salenegg in Maienfeld has made wine since 1068. The Föhn, the warm dry wind from the south, ripens the grapes late into autumn, and the vines sit at about 500 to 650 m on calcareous slate scree. Malans keeps the Completer, a white grape first written down there in 1321.

d.producers_note: 24 winegrowers make Vully AOC on Fribourg and Vaud soil (Région de Fribourg)

vs: The cantonal tables 'Surfaces par commune 2025' and 'Surfaces par cépage 2025' on vs.ch are blocked to automated reading (robots), so commune areas come from the 2025 harvest report, which prints one vineyard surface per commune (sum 4,579.1 ha; BLW 4,577.7 ha) and harvest kg per grape, but no hectares per grape per commune.

Canton grape hectares were read from the Valais column of BLW Weinjahr 2025 tables 1.2/1.3; the PDF text loses empty cells, so only values that are clearly the Valais column were kept (Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc left out). Please check against the PDF.
Grand cru regulation texts not found for Salgesch, Fully, Savièse and Visperterminen; their grape lists come from Artisan Swiss (2019) and Vinum Montis. Leytron's homologation date not found.
Number of grand cru communes: secondary sources say 12 (Artisan Swiss, Vinum Montis, Wine with Seth); swisswine.com says '10 AOC Grand Cru'. Not confirmed by an official list.

No hectares are published for the grand cru parcels; areas are given only for whole communes. The 2015 estimate of about 100 ha for Sierre Grand Cru is journalism (thomasvino), not an official figure.

No Valais premier cru or new cantonal cru framework exists: OVV art. 94 al. 4 bans 'premier cru' and 'cru classé' (text in force 1 April 2026). The 2025/2026 amendment history was not read; amendment tables are not in the consolidated PDF.

The OVV defines no wine regions. Bas-Valais, Valais central and Oberwallis follow Swiss Wine Valais (Port-Valais to Leytron, Chamoson to Sierre, Salgesch to Brig); the assignment of each commune is mine. Older text art. 41 al. 2 (lower sugar minima and commune name rule downstream of Evionnaz) appears repealed ('...') in the 2026 version, not confirmed.
Whether labels may still use former commune names after mergers (Crans-Montana 2017, Noble-Contrée 2021, Sion) was not found in the OVV.
The 1980 zoning decree (RS VS 916.140) splits slopes into zones 1 to 3 for many communes; not used here.
Registered parcel count differs between the French (72,799) and German (7,799) vs.ch pages; left out. Owners 18,225 is on both.
Communes under 20 ha not given their own place (Mont-Noble 18.1, Bovernier 15.5, Port-Valais 14.8, Gampel-Bratsch 12.2, Stalden 12.2, Visp 11.2 and smaller).

ds1: Zürich: the Strickhof reports Rebjahr und Weinlese 2025 and Erntezahlen 2025 in den Gemeinden (redaktion.strickhof.ch GetDokument ids 15861, 15862, 15863, 15867) and the ALN Verfügung über den Rebbau with Anhang 1 (id 607, 16322) could not be fetched (permission not granted / robots). So no official per-commune or per-region Zürich figures: region areas are the rounded Swiss Wine figures, and the five region names are not confirmed as legal Zusatzbezeichnungen.

Zürich: the exact list of Zürich communes entitled to AOC Zürichsee was not read (set by the ALN Verfügung); the outline uses the whole Meilen and Horgen districts. Whether AOC Zürichsee also covers the city of Zürich, Uster, Hinwil, Pfäffikon and Affoltern vineyards is unconfirmed.

Zürich: commune areas exist only from the cantonal Flächenstatistik 2025 (direct-payment land use, codes 0701+0717), and the readable text stopped after Trüllikon, so Stammheim, Andelfingen, Truttikon, Volken and all other districts have no figure. Stäfa is about 40 ha (Weinbauverband). Rafz, Eglisau, Neftenbach and Weiningen have no current area.

Zürich: the 85% commune rule is confirmed only through the Schwyz AOC Zürichsee decree (which must match Zürich law); the Zürich text itself was not read. Grape hectares for Zürich were read from the last cantonal column of the BLW tables 1.2/1.3, which have unmarked blank cells.

Thurgau: the Fachstelle report lists Ortsteile (Iselisberg, Ottenberg, Ottoberg, Nussbaumen, Götighofen, Amlikon). Their match to political communes is from Swiss Wine and Wikipedia (Iselisberg in Uesslingen-Buch, Nussbaumen in Hüttwilen, Ottoberg with Märstetten) and inferred for Ottenberg = Weinfelden and Götighofen = Sulgen. No Weinfelden, Uesslingen-Buch or Märstetten block was found in the text.

Thurgau: Warth-Weiningen 2025 totals were cut off in the extracted text, so its 2024 figure is used. The Anhang 1 production-area list does not name Wigoltingen, Bussnang, Müllheim and other communes with small vineyards; their membership is unknown.
Thurgau: Swiss Wine's six regions (Seebachtal, Unteres Thurtal, Untersee, Rhein, Lauchetal, Oberes Thurtal) are tourist regions; only the three legal production areas are drawn.

Schaffhausen: Osterfingen (merged into Wilchingen 2005) is not in the 2010 boundary set, so it is folded into Wilchingen. Büsingen am Hochrhein (German exclave, 0.72 ha) is in the Reiat/Rhein area by law but has no Swiss boundary. Commune areas use planted (bestockt) area; the overview total 463.48 ha differs slightly from the commune sum 462.14 ha.

Aargau: the 2025 Weinlesebericht with commune figures was not found; commune areas are sums of the 2024 variety rows (the report gives no commune totals). The law does not define regions, so the five regions follow Swiss Wine and are not complete lists. Swiss Wine names Meisterschwanden among the largest Seetal communes, but Liebegg 2024 shows only 0.9 ha.
Aargau: no list of approved Grand Cru Aargau parcels found yet (rule in force since 1 Jan 2025).
Growers per commune are not published in the sources read; Zürich grower total not found in an official source (Falstaff says about 600).
ds2: BLW 2025 per-canton variety tables (1.2/1.3) could not be read column by column (empty cells dropped in the text), so Luzern, Schwyz, Zug, Jura, Glarus and Uri/Obwalden/Nidwalden have no official grape hectares. Luzern Pinot Noir is probably 14.96 ha (first value of the row) but not confirmed.

BLW gives Uri, Obwalden and Nidwalden only together (6.8 ha) and Appenzell AI and AR together (4.45 ha); no separate official 2025 area for UR, OW, NW. AR and AI areas in this file are sums from the LZSG harvest control (3.26 + 0.66 ha).

St. Gallen commune and area figures are sums of the variety rows in the LZSG 2025 harvest control; the communes add to 193.2 ha against 200.2 ha in the cantonal table and 203.7 ha in BLW (difference not explained in the source). Commune grower counts are not published.
LZSG regional report puts Amden and Weesen under 'Übrige Gebiete'; the law (sGS 610.11 Art. 41a) puts them in Sarganserland, which this file follows.

Luzern: the four wine regions (Seetal, Surental/Sempachersee, Vierwaldstättersee, Wiggertal) are in SRL 917 § 2 but without a commune list, so no outlines were drawn. No per-commune area found for Luzern.

Basel-Landschaft has no official wine districts; the Ebenrain list of regional designations and the Reblagenverzeichnis are not published online. Basel-Landschaft canton area by variety: only the top 12 rows read; canton total area not printed in the Herbstbrief.
Uri law RB 60.3231 (Weinreglement) and Jura RSJU 916.141 could not be opened; their label percentages are missing. The Jura AOC label rule is based on the directives and Vinum only.

Zug, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Glarus, Uri and Jura: no per-commune vineyard areas found, so no commune places. Clos des Cantons (Buix, now Basse-Allaine), Weingut Tellen (Kägiswil, Sarnen), Bürglirain (Glarus) and Insel Ufnau not placed: no confirmed coordinates.

The St. Gallen production area is named «Zürichsee» (its legal name) and is separate from the Zürich/Schwyz AOC Zürichsee; parent names Zürichsee vs AOC Zürichsee must not be merged. AOC Zürichsee here covers only the Schwyz communes; it must be merged with the Zürich side if the ZH researcher adds it.

Basel-Stadt: the BS agreement SG 911.200 was not read; the legal link to the BL ordinance rests on the BL text (which names AOC Basel-Stadt) and the CSCV law list. Bettingen has no harvest entry in 2025.
Schwyz growers and Basel-Landschaft growers not published; 'about 400 growers' for St. Gallen is from the growers' association, not a 2025 count.
